note: Commercial acquisition claim registry. Parallel to the residential registry and governed by the same rules: only approvedForPublication=true may enter copy; every claim names the document carrying the operative language; no market statistic without a dated, geography-matched source.
scopeRule: Business capability (what we will consider buying) is recorded in src/data/criteria.ts and is a fact the owner supplies. This registry records only what can be SOURCED. Never convert 'we would consider buying X' into 'we have bought X'.

claims.claim: Boise's I-1 zoning district is intended to accommodate light manufacturing, assembly, fabrication and technology-related uses that may require significant transportation services but typically do not operate at night, and are generally compatible with nearby commercial and residential areas given substantial buffering and screening.
claims.quotedLanguage: The I-1 zoning district is intended to accommodate light manufacturing, assembly, fabrication, and technology-related land uses that may require significant transportation services but that typically do not operate during nighttime hours and are generally compatible with nearby commercial and residential areas when accompanied by substantial buffering, screening, and standards designed to mitigate impacts.
claims.notes: The nighttime-operation and compatibility language is the practical dividing line between I-1 and I-2 for an owner-user or a buyer assessing what a building can be used for. ⚠️ Boise's district; do not generalise to Meridian, Nampa or unincorporated county, none of which have been checked.

claims.claim: Boise's I-2 zoning district accommodates general industrial activity with greater impacts than I-1 — including uses needing significant heavy transportation and uses that frequently operate at night — and the code states the district should be separated from commercial or residential development.
claims.quotedLanguage: The I-2 zoning district is intended to accommodate general industrial activity with greater impacts than those in the I-1 zoning district, including uses that require significant heavy transportation services, uses that frequently operate during nighttime hours, and uses that require additional standards to protect health, safety, or general welfare. The I-2 zoning district should be separated from commercial or residential development.
claims.notes: The separation expectation matters to anyone holding I-2 ground adjacent to housing — it bears on redevelopment and on what a neighbour can object to. It is a statement of intent in the district purpose, NOT a setback requirement; do not present it as a measurable buffer.

claims.claim: Boise's industrial districts do not share a height standard. I-1 Light and I-2 Heavy cap building height at 55 feet with no qualification attached. I-3 Industrial Technology permits 150 feet, but that height is not free-standing: it is controlled by a 45 degree angle of bulk plan measured from all exterior property lines.
claims.quotedLanguage: Controlled by a 45 degree angle of bulk plan from all exterior property lines up to the maximum height of 150 feet.
claims.notes: ⚠️⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-09-10. An earlier version of this claim asserted that BOTH industrial districts cap at 55 ft. Boise has THREE industrial districts, not two, and I-3 permits nearly three times the height. The error came from researching I-1 and I-2 and assuming the set was complete. A page built on the earlier claim would have told an owner of I-3 ground that they were capped at 55 ft. ⚠️ Building height is not clear height. ⚠️ The 150 ft figure carries footnote [3], which has NOT been read — do not present it as unconditional. ⚠️ REWORDED 2026-09-10. The earlier wording, 'I-3 permits up to 150 feet', asserted an outcome the source does not support: the 150 ft cell carries footnote [3], and a full re-read of every cached Boise district page proves the city publishes no footnote definitions at all. The claim now states what the table states and says plainly that the qualification is unread. I-1 and I-2's 55 ft carries no marker and needs no such hedge — the asymmetry between the districts is itself the useful fact. ✅ FOOTNOTE [3] NOW READ (2026-09-10, codified text). The 150 ft figure is real but is shaped by a 45 degree bulk plan from every exterior property line, so the buildable envelope narrows with distance from the boundary and a small parcel cannot reach 150 ft anywhere. ⚠️ Quote it as 'bulk plan' — that is the code's wording, not a typo of ours.

claims.claim: Boise requires a larger parking setback from Interstate frontage in the heavy industrial district than in the light one: any yard adjacent to I-84 or I-184 carries a 10-foot parking setback in I-1 and 20 feet in I-2.
claims.quotedLanguage: Any Yard Adjacent to Interstate (I-84 & I-184) 10 ft.
claims.notes: The quoted language is the I-1 figure; the I-2 page states 20 ft for the same condition. Interstate frontage is the defining feature of much of Boise's industrial ground, so a setback that doubles between districts is a real site-planning input. Both districts also set interior side and rear setbacks at 0 ft, subject to a footnote not yet read.

claims.claim: Boise's I-2 heavy industrial district sets a minimum street frontage of 30 feet, where I-1 sets none.
claims.quotedLanguage: LOT STANDARDS Lot Area (minimum) N/A Street Frontage (minimum) 30 ft.
claims.notes: Neither district sets a minimum lot area, which is worth knowing for small industrial parcels and for splits. The frontage minimum applies in I-2 only.

claims.claim: Idaho and Ada County do not use a single definition of where residential property ends and multifamily or commercial begins. At least three systems draw the line differently: county ASSESSMENT treats residential as up to four units and routes apartments to commercial appraisers; the property condition DISCLOSURE act applies to one to four dwelling units; and the domestic WATER statute excludes apartments, condominiums and similar multiple-dwelling developments generally rather than at a unit count.
claims.notes: ⚠️⚠️ THE CENTRAL MULTIFAMILY FINDING, and the one most likely to be got wrong. There is no single 'multifamily threshold' in Idaho. Assessment says four. Disclosure says one to four. The water statute does not use a unit count at all — it excludes multiple-dwelling developments as a class. Any page stating 'in Idaho, multifamily means 5+ units' would be wrong about at least one of these systems. Always name WHICH system a boundary belongs to. Sources are cross-registry: all three claims live in the residential registry and are re-used here rather than restated.

claims.claim: Ada County's commercial appraisers, not its residential appraisers, value apartments and high-density residential — alongside office, retail and industrial.
claims.quotedLanguage: Our team of commercial appraisers handle valuation for all commercial property types, including, office, retail, industrial, and high-density residential (apartments) uses.
claims.notes: Practical consequence for an owner: an apartment building's assessed value is arrived at by a different team using different methods from a duplex two streets away. The Assessor's page also states that data on construction costs, market sales and INCOME PRODUCTION is used to develop commercial assessments — the income approach appears for commercial and not for residential. ⚠️ QUOTE CORRECTED AND RE-SOURCED 2026-09-10. Two defects, both found the moment the quote audit was extended to cover the commercial registry: the transcription dropped the final word — the county writes '(apartments) uses.' — and the claim cited the real-and-manufactured-property page, which does not contain the sentence at all. It comes from the Assessor's own landing page. The claim was live on a published page while both defects stood.

claims.claim: Ada County develops commercial assessments using data on construction costs, market sales and income production; the residential approach described alongside it relies on construction costs, sales and, where applicable, rental information.
claims.quotedLanguage: Data pertaining to construction costs, market sales, and income-production is used to develop commercial assessments.
claims.notes: Explains why an income-producing property's assessment can move differently from a house's in the same year. ⚠️ Do NOT extrapolate this into a claim about how any specific property was valued, or into cap rate or NOI figures — the page states the inputs, not a methodology document.

claims.claim: Every non-exempt commercial property in Ada County is assessed at market value as of January 1, on the same annual cycle and the same five-year physical inspection requirement as residential property.
claims.quotedLanguage: Idaho law requires that all non-exempt property be assessed at market value as of January 1st.
claims.notes: The Jan 1 lien date and the 5-year inspection cycle are county-wide and asset-class agnostic. Useful for explaining to a commercial owner why an assessment may lag a recent change in the property.

claims.claim: Boise's I-3 Industrial Technology district provides for manufacturing and technological facilities with greater impact than the mixed-use districts allow; the code states such land should be served by major transportation facilities and buffered from adjacent residential areas.
claims.quotedLanguage: The I-3 zoning district is intended to provide for manufacturing and technological facilities that may have a greater impact on the surrounding area than industries allowed in the mixed-use zoning districts. Lands in the I-3 zoning district should be served by major transportation facilities and be buffered from adjacent residential areas.
claims.notes: I-3 is benchmarked against the MIXED-USE districts rather than against I-1/I-2, which is unusual and worth noting: the code positions it as the step up from mixed-use, not as a tier of heavy industrial.

claims.claim: Boise's I-3 district ties its front setback to building height — a minimum of 45 feet plus one additional foot for every foot of building height above 45 feet, or 100 feet — with the street side, interior side and rear yard following the front standard. The 100-foot alternative applies where the property is adjacent to a Residential zoning district or residential use. Where a development forms part of an adopted Industrial Technology master plan, the setbacks apply only to the perimeter of the campus.
claims.quotedLanguage: If a development is part of an adopted Industrial Technology master plan, setbacks shall apply only to the perimeter of the campus.
claims.notes: MATERIALLY IMPORTANT FOR SITE YIELD. The 150 ft height allowance in I-3 is not free — setbacks grow with height on every side, so a taller building consumes substantially more of the parcel. I-1 and I-2 by contrast set interior side and rear at 0 ft. Anyone comparing I-3 to I-1 on height alone is comparing the wrong variable. ⚠️ Footnotes [1] and [2] have not been read; the 'OR 100 ft' alternative is not yet understood and must not be paraphrased. ✅ FOOTNOTES [1] AND [2] NOW READ (2026-09-10, codified text). The 'OR 100 ft' alternative that we previously refused to paraphrase turns out to be the residential-adjacency case. The master-plan provision is the more interesting one commercially: on a campus, interior buildings are not each individually set back, which changes how a large I-3 site can be laid out.

claims.claim: Boise maintains an Airport Influence Area Overlay whose stated purposes include promoting development compatible with and protective of safe airport operation, and ensuring development is compatible with noise levels from airport operations.
claims.quotedLanguage: The purpose of the AI-O district is to: (a) Promote development that is compatible with and protects the safe operation of the airport; (b) Ensure all development is compatible with the noise levels from operations at the airport;
claims.notes: DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO INDUSTRIAL AND DEVELOPMENT GROUND. Much of Boise's industrial land sits near the airport, and an overlay is an additional layer ON TOP of the base zoning — a parcel can be I-1 and AI-O simultaneously, with the overlay adding constraints. ⚠️ Only the purpose clauses have been read; the actual standards have NOT. Do not describe what the overlay requires.

claims.claim: Boise's MX-2 Mixed-Use General district provides for a mix of office, commercial, institutional and residential at a scale serving community needs broader than a nearby neighbourhood, with building height capped at 45 feet and front setbacks set as a range of minimum 0 to maximum 20 feet.
claims.quotedLanguage: The MX-2 district is intended to provide opportunities for a mix of office, commercial, institutional, and residential at a scale designed to serve community needs broader than those of nearby neighborhoods.
claims.notes: A MAXIMUM front setback is a different regulatory instrument from a minimum — it pushes buildings toward the street rather than merely keeping them off it, which constrains surface parking placement. Boise has SEVEN mixed-use districts (active, downtown, general, health, neighborhood, TOD node, university); only MX-2 has been read.

claims.claim: Boise's R-3 Residential Urban district states no maximum density. Its codified table gives a minimum lot area of 1,500 square feet for single-family attached and 2,000 square feet for all other uses, a 20-foot average lot width, a 20-foot minimum street frontage, and a density maximum of N/A.
claims.quotedLanguage: LOT STANDARDS [1] Lot Area (minimum) Single-Family Attached: 1,500 sf. All Other Uses: 2,000 sf. Lot Width (average) 20 ft. Street Frontage (minimum) 20 ft. Density (maximum) N/A
claims.notes: ✅ RESTORED 2026-09-10 from the codified table, having been withdrawn for good reason. Both original defects are resolved and both were real: the lot area is 2,000 sf (the City's webpage prints '2,00 sf', a typo on their page), and the density cell carries NO footnote marker in the code at all — the markers on the City's summary page sit on different rows than the code's do. The code's four notes attach to LOT STANDARDS, interior side, the 5-or-10-foot figure, and rear. ⚠️ No stated maximum density is NOT unlimited density: minimum lot area, setbacks and the four-storey/50-foot height cap all still bind, as does anything outside this table.

claims.claim: Ada County's adopted zoning ordinance establishes eighteen base districts and eight overlay districts. Its commercial and industrial base districts are Limited Office (LO), Neighborhood Commercial (C1), Community Commercial (C2), Light Industrial (M1), General Industrial (M2) and Airport Industrial (M3), alongside a Planned Community (PC) district and ten residential and rural districts.
claims.quotedLanguage: 8-2-16: LIMITED OFFICE (LO) 8-2-17: NEIGHBORHOOD COMMERCIAL (C1) 8-2-18: COMMUNITY COMMERCIAL (C2) 8-2-19: LIGHT INDUSTRIAL (M1) 8-2-20: GENERAL INDUSTRIAL (M2) 8-2-21: AIRPORT INDUSTRIAL (M3) 8-2-22: PLANNED COMMUNITY (PC)
claims.notes: ✅ UNBLOCKED 2026-09-10 after nine days withheld. It was held because the only county text we had was a PDF whose ordinance number line read literally 'ORDINANCE NO. _____' with a PZ_JAN2025 filename — a draft to the Planning and Zoning Commission, not adopted law. The adopted text is Ordinance No. 1002, published by the Ada County Clerk, and the district schedule in it matches what the draft showed. Two independent confirmations of adoption: the ordinance carries a real number, and a later county ordinance of 27 May 2026 amends the zoning map of 'TITLE 8 OF ADA COUNTY CODE, AS ADOPTED BY ORDINANCE NO. 1002'. Withholding it for nine days was correct — the draft could have changed before adoption, and publishing a district schedule that later moved would have been worse than saying nothing. ⚠️ temporalStatus CORRECTED 2026-09-10 from ADOPTION_UNCONFIRMED to CURRENT. When this claim was unblocked against Ordinance No. 1002 the claim text, quote, sources, confidence, approval and verification flag were all updated and this field was not — so an APPROVED, live claim carried a status saying its adoption was unconfirmed, contradicting its own notes. Not visible to a reader (the field was never emitted to the app) but wrong in the registry, which is where the next person looks.

claims.claim: Ada County and the City of Boise use entirely different zoning vocabularies for the same kinds of property. The county's adopted code calls its industrial districts M1 Light Industrial, M2 General Industrial and M3 Airport Industrial; Boise calls its I-1 Light Industrial, I-2 Heavy Industrial and I-3 Industrial Technology. The county's commercial districts are LO, C1 and C2; Boise's equivalents sit in its mixed-use MX series. A parcel does not change character at a city limit, but the code governing it does.
claims.quotedLanguage: 8-2-19: LIGHT INDUSTRIAL (M1) 8-2-20: GENERAL INDUSTRIAL (M2) 8-2-21: AIRPORT INDUSTRIAL (M3)
claims.notes: ✅ UNBLOCKED 2026-09-10 against the adopted Ordinance No. 1002. A genuine trap for owners and one no competitor addresses: 'light industrial' is M1 in unincorporated Ada County and I-1 in Boise, and they are different districts under different codes with different standards. ⚠️ NEVER carry a Boise standard across a city limit, in either direction. This claim establishes that the vocabularies differ; it does NOT establish that any particular standard corresponds. ⚠️ temporalStatus CORRECTED 2026-09-10 from ADOPTION_UNCONFIRMED to CURRENT. When this claim was unblocked against Ordinance No. 1002 the claim text, quote, sources, confidence, approval and verification flag were all updated and this field was not — so an APPROVED, live claim carried a status saying its adoption was unconfirmed, contradicting its own notes. Not visible to a reader (the field was never emitted to the app) but wrong in the registry, which is where the next person looks.

claims.claim: Boise's MX-5 Mixed-Use Downtown district states no maximum building height, where every other Boise district read so far carries one: MX-2 at 45 feet, R-3 at four stories not exceeding 50 feet, I-1 and I-2 at 55 feet, and I-3 at 150 feet.
claims.quotedLanguage: HEIGHT (MAXIMUM) D Building Height N/A
claims.notes: MATERIALLY IMPORTANT FOR DOWNTOWN REDEVELOPMENT GROUND, and a genuine outlier in the code. ⚠️ Unlike R-3's density cell, which reads 'N./A' with footnotes [2][3] attached, the MX-5 height cell carries NO footnote marker — which is why this is recorded at HIGH confidence and R-3's density is not. Height is nonetheless constrained in practice by other code provisions not yet read (design review, the Capitol Boulevard Design Overlay, airport influence). Never write 'you can build to any height downtown'. The accurate statement is that the DISTRICT states no maximum.

claims.claim: Boise's MX-5 district provides for a mix of higher-intensity office, commercial, institutional and residential uses, is intended to serve the Downtown Planning Area defined in the Comprehensive Plan, and sets front and side-street setbacks as a range of minimum 0 to maximum 20 feet with interior side and rear minimums of 0 feet.
claims.quotedLanguage: The MX-5 district is intended to provide opportunities for a mix of higher intensity office, commercial, institutional, and residential uses. The MX-5 district is intended to accommodate the needs of the city's Downtown Planning Area as defined in the Comprehensive Plan and to provide for activities conducive to a compact, concentrated, and walkable urban downtown mixed-use center.
claims.notes: The district explicitly references the Downtown Planning Area 'as defined in the Comprehensive Plan' — a direct instance of zoning depending on a comprehensive-plan designation, which is why zoning and future land use must never be treated as interchangeable.

claims.claim: Boise's MX-4 district supports transit-oriented development concentrated at identified transit stations, and the city states the district will be expanded as new best-in-class transit routes are added and stations identified.
claims.quotedLanguage: The MX-4 district is intended to provide opportunities for a mix of office, commercial, institutional, and residential uses to support transit. This zoning district will require transit-oriented development concentrated at identified transit stations. This zoning district will be expanded as new investments in best-in-class transit routes are added and transit stations identified.
claims.notes: An EXPANDING district by the city's own statement — the map is expected to change as transit investment lands. That is a freshness hazard: any page naming MX-4 extent will go stale. Record as a periodic-revalidation claim and never state where MX-4 currently applies.

claims.claim: Boise maintains a Flood Protection Overlay whose stated purpose recognises that the city's flood hazard areas are subject to periodic inundation, and that flood losses are caused both by natural forces and by construction practices that increase flood heights and velocities, and by structures inadequately anchored or flood-proofed.
claims.quotedLanguage: The flood hazard areas of Boise City are subject to periodic inundation, which may result in loss of life and property, health and safety hazards, disruption of commerce and government services, extraordinary public expenditures for flood protection and relief, and impairment of the tax base, all of which adversely affect the public health, safety, and general welfare.
claims.notes: Pairs with the already-established fact that Boise's flood exposure has three sources (Boise River, foothills gulches, upper-bench intermittent channels) and that any floodplain development requires a permit. ⚠️ Only the purpose clauses are read. The overlay's actual standards are NOT known and must not be described.

claims.claim: Idaho Code § 63-307A does not exist. Title 63, Chapter 3 runs from 63-301 to 63-316 with no 63-307A, and 63-307 governs ownership identification rather than sale price. The section number traces to Senate Bill 1196 of the 2007 session, which proposed a property transfer certificate requiring purchasers to disclose sales prices to county assessors; the bill's recorded history shows only introduction, printing and referral to the Local Government committee, with no further action.
claims.quotedLanguage: 63-307. Ownership identification. (1) The assessor shall ascertain the current ownership of land from documents recorded in the county recorder's office and/or from evidence of ownership furnished to the assessor that is admissible at trial in a civil action.
claims.notes: 🚨🚨 FABRICATION GUARD — NOT FOR PUBLICATION, FOR INTERNAL PROTECTION. A research pass surfaced a confident, richly detailed description of 'Idaho Code 63-307A' — property transfer certificate, confidentiality, civil and criminal penalties, and a closed list of who may view it (Idaho appraisers, real estate licensees, the Tax Commission, anyone owning 5%+ of the property, and tax appeal bodies). That description matches the PROPOSED TEXT OF SB 1196 (2007), not enacted law. Verified independently: the chapter index has no 63-307A, and the bill died after referral to committee. This is the same failure mode as Missouri's phantom contract-for-deed statute caught on MoKan — a non-existent section laundered through repetition until it reads as settled law. NEVER cite 63-307A. If any future draft references it, this claim is the reason it must be removed. ⚠️ CORROBORATED 2026-09-10 by reading the full Title 63 Chapter 3 section index directly: it runs 63-306, 63-307 (OWNERSHIP IDENTIFICATION), 63-308. There is no 63-307A. The index is cached.

claims.claim: No Idaho statute requires a buyer or seller of real property to disclose the sale price to the county assessor. The assessor is directed to ascertain OWNERSHIP from recorded documents; the statute says nothing about price, and the 2007 bill that would have created a price-disclosure certificate for residential property was introduced and referred to committee without further action.
claims.quotedLanguage: The assessor shall ascertain the current ownership of land from documents recorded in the county recorder's office and/or from evidence of ownership furnished to the assessor that is admissible at trial in a civil action.
claims.notes: 🚨 WITHHELD. This is potentially the single most valuable fact in the entire commercial vertical — if Idaho sale prices are not public record, commercial comparables are structurally unavailable to an owner, which explains WHY a seller cannot self-serve a valuation and reframes the whole proposition. But it is a NEGATIVE claim ('no statute requires X'), and proving a negative from two sections plus one dead bill is not sufficient. A search of 63-307 and the Chapter 3 index is not a search of the whole code. BEFORE PUBLISHING: search Title 63 exhaustively for any disclosure or transfer-declaration requirement, check Title 55 conveyancing, and reconcile against the Ada County Assessor's own statement that commercial assessments use 'market sales' data — if prices are not disclosed, the Assessor must obtain sales some other way, and how they do it is itself the most citable part of this story. ✅ SUPERSEDED 2026-09-10 and permanently retired, not resurrected. It was framed as a negative — 'no statute requires disclosure' — which cannot be proven by reading a handful of sections, and so it sat withheld while being the most valuable fact we held. The fix was to stop trying to prove the negative: idaho-recorded-documents-are-public, idaho-deed-content-requirement-omits-price, idaho-is-a-non-disclosure-state and idaho-assessor-records-conditional-confidentiality say the same thing affirmatively, each from a source that states it directly. Keep this row as the record of why negative claims are a trap.

claims.claim: The federal housing-finance definition that produces the familiar 1-4 versus 5+ split is in FHFA regulation: multifamily housing means a residence consisting of more than four dwelling units, and single-family housing means a residence consisting of one to four dwelling units.
claims.quotedLanguage: Multifamily housing means a residence consisting of more than four dwelling units. … Single-family housing means a residence consisting of one to four dwelling units.
claims.notes: THIS is the actual origin of the '5+ units is commercial' folk rule — a MORTGAGE-FINANCE boundary, not a general legal one. ⚠️ It governs housing-finance classification. It does NOT make a five-unit building 'legally commercial' for zoning, assessment, disclosure or any Idaho purpose. Never write 'in Idaho, 5+ units is commercial'.

claims.claim: The U.S. Census Bureau treats a two-unit structure as multifamily. Its Building Permits Survey tabulates one-unit structures, then 2 units, 3 and 4 units combined, and 5 or more units — so five is where Census stops disaggregating, not where multifamily begins. The American Community Survey uses brackets of 1 detached, 1 attached, 2, 3 or 4, 5 to 9, 10 to 19, 20 to 49, and 50 or more.
claims.quotedLanguage: Multifamily structures are classified by the number of housing units in the structure. Data are tabulated for 2 units, 3 and 4 units combined, and 5 or more unit structures.
claims.notes: DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS the folk rule. In Census terms a DUPLEX is multifamily. 5+ is a tabulation bracket and carries no residential/commercial meaning at all. The ACS also defines a structure as separated from others by dividing walls ground to roof, counts occupied and vacant units alike, and EXCLUDES stores and office space from the unit count.

claims.claim: HUD has no single multifamily unit threshold. Its Section 207, 221(d)(4) and 223(f) programmes require five or more units, but Section 220 in urban renewal areas reaches two or more units and Section 231 rental housing for the elderly requires eight or more.
claims.quotedLanguage: Such property or project may include five or more family units and may include such commercial and community facilities as the Secretary deems adequate to serve the occupants.
claims.notes: NEGATIVE FINDING and a valuable one: even inside a single federal agency the threshold moves between 2, 5 and 8 depending on the programme. The quoted language is the National Housing Act §207 at 12 U.S.C. §1713(c), which is the statutory root of the '5 or more family units' figure. Anyone asserting a single HUD definition is wrong.

claims.claim: At least six systems draw the residential/multifamily line differently, and no two of them agree in scope: Ada County assessment routes properties above four units to commercial appraisers; Idaho's disclosure act covers one to four dwelling units; Idaho's domestic water statute excludes multiple-dwelling developments with no unit count at all; the Census treats two units as multifamily and uses five only as a tabulation bracket; FHFA defines multifamily as more than four dwelling units for housing finance; and HUD's own programmes use two, five or eight depending on the programme.
claims.notes: ⭐ THE FLAGSHIP MULTIFAMILY CLAIM. This is the page nobody else in this market can write, because it requires six primary sources across county, state and federal authority. The correct framing is: the '5+ units is commercial' rule is a MORTGAGE-FINANCE convention (FHFA) that has been generalised far beyond its scope. It is not an Idaho legal boundary, it is not a Census boundary, and it is not even a consistent HUD boundary. ⚠️ A page on this must NEVER conclude that five units is 'legally commercial' — it must say which system each boundary governs. Note also NO Idaho statute found so far uses a five-unit threshold for real property; Idaho consistently uses one to four.

claims.claim: The observed search boundary between residential and commercial multifamily intent in Boise coincides with the federal housing-finance boundary: commercial marketplaces rank on apartment-building queries and are absent from rental-property queries, while residential direct buyers rank on rental-property queries and are absent from apartment-building queries. The overlap between the two is the two-to-four unit range — the same range FHFA classifies as single-family housing.
claims.notes: 🚨 INTERNAL STRATEGY ONLY — NEVER PUBLISHED AS A FACT ABOUT THE WORLD. This is an observation about search results on one date, not a property of Idaho real estate. SERPs move. Its value is architectural: it tells us where to draw the line between residential and commercial pages, and it happens to agree with the FHFA four-unit boundary, which is a genuine reason to expect the split to be stable. Recorded VOLATILE and withheld from publication permanently.

claims.claim: Boise's R-3 Residential Urban district caps building height at four stories not to exceed 50 feet.
claims.quotedLanguage: HEIGHT (MAXIMUM) D Building Height 4 stories not to exceed 50 ft.
claims.notes: Split out of the withdrawn boise-r3-no-maximum-density. This cell is safe where the rest of that table is not: the HEIGHT (MAXIMUM) row carries NO footnote marker, whereas the LOT STANDARDS block carries [1], the lot-area and density cells carry [2] and [3], and the setback rows carry [3][4][5]. Height is the only R-3 standard we can read to completion from a public source. ⚠️ Two stories of constraint sit outside the table and are not covered by this claim: a height allowance is not a density allowance, and it is not an entitlement.

claims.claim: The City of Boise's online zoning district pages reproduce each district's dimensional standards table together with its bracketed footnote markers, but do not publish the footnote definitions those markers point to. As accessed on 10 September 2026, the R-3 table carried markers [1] through [5], the I-3 table carried [1] through [3], and the I-1 and I-2 tables carried [1], and no definition for any of them appeared on any of those pages.
claims.quotedLanguage: LOT STANDARDS [1] Lot Area (minimum) [2] Single-Family Attached: 1,500 sf. All Other Uses: 2,00 sf. Lot Width (average) 20 ft. Street Frontage (minimum) 20 ft. Density (maximum) [2][3] N./A
claims.notes: Established by re-reading all eleven cached Boise district pages and searching each for a footnote definition. None has one. This is materially useful to an owner and no competitor says it: the number on the city's website is not necessarily the number that governs the parcel, and a setback of '0 ft. [1]' is not a setback of zero. It also explains why several of our own claims are withheld rather than weak. The same quoted line carries a second, separate observation worth keeping: the city's R-3 lot-area cell is printed '2,00 sf', so even the digits on the page cannot be taken at face value. ⚠️ VOLATILE — this is a fact about a website on one date. Re-verify before relying on it, and never state it as a criticism; state it as a reason to read the code.

claims.claim: Boise's I-1 and I-2 industrial tables set minimum interior side and rear yard setbacks at zero feet, but only away from housing. Where the property is adjacent to a Residential zoning district or a residential use, the minimum becomes 30 feet for development under three acres, 50 feet between three and ten acres, and 100 feet for development of ten or more acres. Front is 20 feet and street side 15 feet in both districts.
claims.quotedLanguage: When adjacent to a Residential zoning district or residential use, 30 ft. minimum for all development under three acres, 50 ft. minimum for all development between three acres and 10 acres, and 100 ft. minimum for all development of 10 or more acres.
claims.notes: ⚠️⚠️ MATERIALLY CORRECTED 2026-09-10, and it had already reached a published page. The earlier version reported a bare zero-foot setback with an unreadable footnote. The footnote is not a technicality: next to housing the setback scales with development size to as much as 100 feet, which can dominate the yield of an industrial site. An owner told 'zero' would have been badly misled. The footnote is identical in I-1 (Table 11-02.27) and I-2 (Table 11-02.29) and applies to the parking setbacks as well as the building setbacks. This is why a footnoted cell may never be paraphrased.

claims.claim: Idaho law does not require an assessment to match market value exactly. It requires that the median ratio of assessed value to market value, for each category of property tested, fall within a range of 90 percent to 110 percent of market value, tested with statistical methods, and that categories be within five percentage points of one another.
claims.quotedLanguage: The recognized appraisal methods shall, at a minimum, require the assessment of such property to reflect, within reasonable statistical certainty, the median ratio of assessed value to market value for the categories of property being tested within a range of ninety percent (90%) to one hundred ten percent (110%) of market value
claims.notes: This is the honest way to say an assessed value is not a transaction price, and it does not require criticising anyone: the statute sets its own tolerance, and it is a band rather than a point. ⚠️ The band is a MEDIAN across a CATEGORY, not a guarantee about an individual parcel — a single property can sit well outside it while the county is fully compliant. Never write that an assessment is accurate to within ten percent.

claims.claim: Idaho requires every taxable property to be appraised at least once every five years, on a rolling schedule reaching fifteen percent of a county's properties in year one and one hundred percent by year five. In the years between appraisals, a property is indexed to current market value using market value property transactions rather than individually appraised.
claims.quotedLanguage: Annually, all taxable property, not appraised that year, shall be indexed to reflect current market value for assessment purposes using market value property transactions and results of the annual appraisal of taxable property.
claims.notes: MATERIALLY IMPORTANT and almost never said out loud to owners. An assessed value may be as much as five years from the last time anyone appraised that specific property; the intervening years are an index applied to a class. For a commercial building whose income has changed materially since its last appraisal, that gap is the whole explanation of why the assessor's number and a transaction price diverge — without anyone having made a mistake. ⚠️ Do not tell a reader their own assessment is stale. We do not know when their parcel was last appraised, and § 63-314 requires the assessor to keep records showing exactly that.

claims.claim: Idaho sets the assessment date by statute at 12:01 a.m. on the first day of January of the year the taxes are levied, for all real, personal and operating property subject to property taxation.
claims.quotedLanguage: All real, personal and operating property subject to property taxation must be assessed annually at market value for assessment purposes as of 12:01 a.m. of the first day of January in the year in which such property taxes are levied, except as otherwise provided.
claims.notes: The statutory basis for what we previously held only from the Ada County Assessor's own webpage. A statute is a stronger source than a county explainer and does not go stale when a website is redesigned. Read together with idaho-appraisal-cycle-five-years, this is the complete answer to why an assessment is not a price: a fixed date, a tolerance band, and up to five years since anyone looked.

claims.claim: Every commercial and industrial district in Ada County's adopted zoning ordinance carries the same stated purpose: to encourage those uses primarily inside areas of impact, implementing the comprehensive plans adopted as part of the area of impact agreements, and to be established outside an area of impact only on a limited basis. The district's allowed uses turn on the availability of urban public facilities and the applicable comprehensive plan designation.
claims.quotedLanguage: The General Industrial (M2) District promotes the public health, safety, and welfare of Ada County by encouraging industrial uses primarily inside areas of impact to implement the applicable comprehensive plans that are adopted as part of the area of impact agreements. The General Industrial (M2) District may also be established outside areas of impact on a limited basis.
claims.notes: MATERIALLY IMPORTANT AND EASY TO MISS. County commercial and industrial zoning is written around city AREAS OF IMPACT — the county is not planning a parallel industrial economy, it is holding ground that a city's comprehensive plan expects to absorb. For an owner of unincorporated commercial or industrial ground this shapes what is realistically permitted and what happens on annexation. The identical purpose language repeats verbatim across LO, C1, C2, M1, M2 and M3, so this is a structural feature of the code rather than a quirk of one district. ⚠️ Says nothing about whether any particular parcel WILL be annexed, and nothing about timing.

claims.claim: Idaho county recorder records are fully open. Every book of record, map, chart, survey and other paper on file must be open during office hours to any person who wishes to inspect it, without charge.
claims.quotedLanguage: All books of record, maps, charts, surveys and other papers on file in the recorder's office, must, during office hours, be open for the inspection of any person who may desire to inspect them, and may be inspected without charge
claims.notes: ESSENTIAL CONTEXT, and it must be published ALONGSIDE the non-disclosure claim rather than instead of it. The barrier in Idaho is not secrecy and not access — access is total and free. The price simply is not in the document. Publishing 'Idaho hides sale prices' would be wrong and would also miss what is actually interesting.

claims.claim: Idaho states what a conveyance of real property must contain: a written instrument, subscribed by the party disposing of the property or an authorised agent, and the grantee's name and complete mailing address. The price is not among the required elements.
claims.quotedLanguage: A conveyance of an estate in real property may be made by an instrument in writing, subscribed by the party disposing of the same, or by his agent thereunto authorized by writing. The name of the grantee and his complete mailing address must appear on such instrument.
claims.notes: ⚠️ WORDING IS LOAD-BEARING. The statute is SILENT on price — it neither requires nor forbids stating one. The affirmative, provable fact is only that price is not among the elements the statute requires. Never write that Idaho deeds 'do not state' or 'may not state' a price; that is an inference the statute does not support, and some deeds do recite consideration. This is the affirmative route around what was previously an unprovable negative claim.

claims.claim: Idaho is a non-disclosure state. County assessors say so in their own words and describe the consequence: they depend on the public to volunteer sales information when property changes hands, because no law requires it to be reported.
claims.quotedLanguage: Since Idaho is a non-disclosure state, the Assessor's office depends heavily on the public to provide sales and cost information.
claims.notes: 🎯 THE SINGLE MOST VALUABLE FACT IN THIS VERTICAL, and it took converting an unprovable negative into an affirmative one to publish it. It was withheld for days as 'no statute requires disclosure' — a negative that cannot be proven from reading a few sections. The route through was to stop trying: two county assessors state the characterisation affirmatively, in their own words, and describe the operational consequence. ⚠️ The quoted wording is BONNER County's; Canyon County's is near-identical but says 'sales information when property is bought and sold'. ⚠️ NEITHER IS ADA COUNTY. They are cited for a statewide characterisation of Idaho law, which is what they assert. Ada County's own assessor pages do not use the phrase. ⚠️ Always publish with idaho-recorded-documents-are-public: access to the record is total and free; the price is simply not in it.

claims.claim: Idaho exempts certain assessor records from public disclosure, including confidential commercial or financial information, but the exemption is not automatic: the taxpayer must claim it by stamping or marking the documents. The information that is always disclosable includes the owner's name and mailing address, the parcel number, the legal description, square footage and acreage, the assessed value, the tax district and rate, and the total property tax.
claims.quotedLanguage: it shall be the responsibility of the taxpayer to give notice of its claim to exemption by stamping or marking each page or the first page of each portion of documents so claimed
claims.notes: ⚠️ MEDIUM on purpose, and it must never be flattened into 'sale prices are confidential in Idaho'. This exemption is CONDITIONAL — it depends on a taxpayer actively claiming it — and it covers commercial and financial information in assessor records, not sale prices as such. Its real value is the contrast in the always-disclosable list: ASSESSED VALUE is public, and a transaction price is not on the list at all. That is why an owner can look up their assessment in seconds and cannot look up what the building down the street sold for.

claims.claim: Net operating income is the income from a property's operations available for repayment of debt and return on equity to the owner, after deducting economic vacancy and all expenses, excluding debt service.
claims.quotedLanguage: Net Operating Income is the income from a property's operations available for repayment of debt and return on equity to the owner after deducting economic vacancy and all expenses (exclusive of debt service).
claims.notes: Sourced from a GSE's Seller/Servicer Guide glossary — binding contract vocabulary for lenders originating multifamily loans — rather than from a brokerage explainer. That distinction was the whole reason this sat unwritten: the vocabulary gate requires rent roll, NOI and cap rate on the commercial pages to keep them from being classified as residential, but a definition sourced to a broker's marketing glossary is not a definition. ⚠️ The exclusion of debt service is the part owners most often get wrong: NOI is a property-level figure and is indifferent to how the property is financed.

claims.claim: A capitalization rate is the percentage rate representing the relationship between the value of a property and the net operating income it produces.
claims.quotedLanguage: The Capitalization Rate is the percentage rate that represents the proper relationship between the value of the Property and the Net Operating Income that the Property produces.
claims.notes: ⚠️ THE DEFINITION IS PUBLISHABLE. A RATE IS NOT. Stating what a capitalization rate IS carries no valuation implication; stating what cap rates ARE in Boise is an undated market statistic and is machine-rejected, and working an example with numbers a reader could mistake for their own situation is a prohibited implicit appraisal. See COMMERCIAL-VALUATION-EDUCATION-MODEL.md §6. ⚠️ Note the direction of the relationship as the Guide states it: the rate expresses a relationship between value and income. It is not a thing that exists independently and is then applied.

claims.claim: Idaho's architects chapter does not apply to architectural services for a building used as a single or multiple family residence not exceeding three units or three stories in height. The exemption stops at three units, so a fourplex sits above it and a triplex does not — a boundary at three, in a state where other systems draw the line at two, four or five.
claims.quotedLanguage: The rendering of any architectural service required in the erection, enlargement, alteration or repair of any building, where the building is to be or is used as a single or multiple family residence not exceeding three (3) units or three (3) stories in height
claims.notes: ⚠️ WORDED AS AN EXEMPTION, WHICH IS WHAT THE STATUTE IS. § 54-306 lists what the architects chapter does NOT reach; it does not itself say 'an architect is required'. Saying the exemption ends at three units is exactly supported; saying 'a fourplex requires an architect' is a step beyond the text and must not be written. STRENGTHENS the boundary argument considerably: this is a SEVENTH system, and it puts the line at THREE — a number no other system in the set uses. It also lands inside the two-to-four range where residential and commercial search intent overlap, which is a nice demonstration that the ambiguity is real rather than rhetorical.

claims.claim: The City of Boise's zoning district webpages are summaries and differ from the codified ordinance in ways that matter. They reproduce the dimensional tables and their bracketed markers but publish no footnote definitions, so the I-1 page shows an interior side setback of "0 ft. [1]" and the I-3 page a building height of "150 ft. [3]" without the qualifications those markers point to. In the R-3 table the markers sit on different rows than the code places them, and the minimum lot area for all other uses is printed as "2,00 sf" where the code reads 2,000 square feet.
claims.quotedLanguage: Lot Width (average) 20 ft. Street Frontage (minimum) 20 ft. Density (maximum) N/A
claims.notes: Supersedes the weaker boise-district-pages-omit-footnote-definitions in usefulness, and both are true. Established by reading the codified table and the city page side by side. ⚠️ Write it as a reason to read the ordinance, NEVER as a criticism of the city — a summary table is a reasonable thing for a planning department to publish, and the code is one click away from it. ⚠️ VOLATILE: this is a fact about a website on one date.

claims.claim: Across the Treasure Valley, the setback that actually governs a commercial or industrial parcel is usually the one measured against housing — and no two cities express it the same way. Boise's I-1 and I-2 print a zero-foot interior side and rear yard that becomes 30, 50 or 100 feet next to a residential district or use depending on the size of the development. Star requires a minimum of 15 feet in its CBD, C-1, C-2, LO, IL, PS, RC and M-U zones when adjacent to a residential use or zone. Kuna does something different again: the setback becomes whatever the adjacent residential district itself requires.
claims.quotedLanguage: When a commercial and/or industrial use abuts a residential zoning district, the yard setback requirements shall be the same as required in the adjacent residential district. When residents are located in commercial or industrial zones, the yard setbacks are the same as required for the R-4 residential zoning district.
claims.notes: 🎯 THE STRONGEST CROSS-JURISDICTION FINDING WE HOLD, and no competitor content addresses it. Three cities, three mechanisms, one shared reality: the number in the dimensional table is not the number that governs a parcel that touches housing. Boise scales it by development acreage, Star sets a flat floor, Kuna makes the commercial parcel inherit the residential district's own requirement. ⚠️ It is a claim about a PATTERN, not a formula. Never compute a setback for a reader from it, and never carry one city's number to another — the whole point is that they differ. Each component is separately quoted and cached; the quoted language here is Kuna's, which is the most surprising of the three. ⚠️ DO NOT GENERALISE 'Kuna prints N/A'. Only C-2, C-3, CBD, M-1, M-2 and P carry N/A setbacks; Kuna's C-1 carries real figures. The inheritance provision is what N/A resolves to in those districts, not a description of Kuna's whole table.

claims.claim: Star's Light Industrial district requires all mechanical equipment emissions, shipping and delivery, and other outdoor activity areas to sit at least three hundred feet from any abutting residential district, or the use becomes subject to a conditional use permit.
claims.quotedLanguage: All mechanical equipment emissions; shipping and/or delivery; or other outdoor activity areas shall be located a minimum of three hundred feet (300') from any abutting residential districts, or the use is subject to a conditional use permit.
claims.notes: MATERIALLY IMPORTANT AND EASY TO MISS, because it is not a setback and does not appear in the dimensional table. It constrains where OPERATIONS can happen on the site rather than where the building sits, and 300 feet is far enough to render part of a small parcel unusable for loading. ⚠️ Note the escape: it is not a prohibition, it triggers a conditional use permit. Never write that the use is banned. ⚠️ Star's code names this district BOTH ways — 'LI' in § 8-3A-1 and 'IL' in Table 8-3A-4. That is the code's own inconsistency, not a transcription error of ours.

claims.claim: Garden City's C-2 is a mixed use commercial district, not a general commercial one. That inverts the convention in neighbouring cities, where C-2 denotes a commercial district — Star and Kuna both use C-2 for commercial and place mixed use elsewhere. Garden City's only industrial district is LI Light Industrial, with a 55-foot height maximum, while the height cell for its C-1 and C-2 districts is left blank in the table.
claims.quotedLanguage: Mixed use commercial (C-2)
claims.notes: A LIVE TRAP for anyone normalising district codes across the valley, which is exactly what a national template would do. C-2 means one thing in Garden City and something else a few miles away. ⚠️ MEDIUM confidence and a hard limit on wording: the height cell for C-1 and C-2 is GENUINELY BLANK in the codified table — no value, no marker, no footnote, verified cell by cell in the raw HTML. That is NOT the Boise situation of an unreachable footnote. Never state or imply a height limit for those districts, and never describe the blank as 'no maximum' — we do not know what it means and the code does not say. ⚠️ assetClass includes industrial because the claim states Garden City’s only industrial district and its height maximum; the TOPIC list deliberately does NOT include "industrial", so this cannot inflate the industrial page’s differentiation count. It is context, not a differentiator.

claims.claim: Eagle expands its side setback with building storeys rather than with proximity to housing. Except for single-family attached dwellings, a multi-storey structure requires an additional five feet of side setback per storey, in every district including its M-1, BP, M-2 and M-3 industrial districts, whose tables otherwise show a zero-foot interior side. Eagle also requires residential buildings located in non-residential districts to meet the residential height and area regulations.
claims.quotedLanguage: Except for single-family attached dwellings, an additional 5 feet per story side setback is required for multi-story structures. Height not to exceed maximum allowed within the zone.
claims.notes: A FOURTH MECHANISM, and it broadens the pattern rather than repeating it. Boise, Star and Kuna all expand the setback according to PROXIMITY TO HOUSING; Eagle expands it according to the BUILDING'S OWN HEIGHT, and does so in every district. So the honest generalisation is not 'the setback next to housing is the one that governs' — it is that a tabled setback is the UNCONSTRAINED case and several different kinds of condition enlarge it. ⚠️ Condition B rides the setback columns for every row of § 8-2-4 via the header marker, which is why it reaches the industrial districts at all — that is not obvious from reading an industrial row on its own. ⚠️ Eagle's conditions F, I and J are residential-only by their own terms and H has nothing to act on in the industrial rows, whose lot area reads n/a. ⚠️ CONDITION C IS A THIRD MECHANISM AGAIN and the cleanest example of the whole argument: 'All residential buildings in other than agricultural or residential districts must meet residential official height and area regulations.' That is the district's standards being displaced by the USE, not by adjacency and not by height. An M-1 parcel carrying a residential building is not governed by the M-1 row at all.

claims.claim: Meridian sets a single set of dimensional standards for both of its industrial districts, I-L and I-H: front, rear and interior side setbacks of zero feet, a street setback of 35 feet, and a maximum building height of 50 feet. The table does not present those figures as final — its own text directs the reader to exceptions and clarifications set out elsewhere in the code.
claims.quotedLanguage: Table 11-2C-3 of this subsection shall be used for determining required setbacks, street and use landscape buffers and maximum building height standards for development in each of the industrial districts. Subsection (A)(2) of this section and subsection 11-3B-7.C.1.c of this title sets forth certain exceptions and additional clarification for the dimensional standards.
claims.notes: The best single piece of evidence for the whole 'a tabled figure is the start of the analysis' argument, because MERIDIAN SAYS IT ITSELF, in the table's own preamble, rather than us inferring it from four cities. ⚠️ The exceptions at 11-3B-7.C.1.c have NOT been read, so nothing may be said about what they require — only that the code says they exist. ⚠️ Meridian's industrial height of 50 ft is LOWER than Boise's I-1/I-2 at 55 ft and far below I-3's 150 ft; do not carry a Boise height across the city limit. ⚠️ Meridian's zoningmap.pdf is a city publication, not codified — never cite a number to it.

claims.claim: The designation M-3 does not mean one thing across the Treasure Valley. In unincorporated Ada County it is Airport Industrial, a live district in the adopted zoning ordinance. In Eagle it is Extractive Industrial, for the mining, processing and storage of mineral resources. In Kuna it was limited to mining uses and has been consolidated into M-2, so it no longer operates. Boise has no M-3 at all — its third industrial district is I-3 Industrial Technology, for technology and research uses.
claims.quotedLanguage: M-3 EXTRACTIVE INDUSTRIAL DISTRICT: To provide land for the mining, processing and storage of mineral resources.
claims.notes: 🎯 THE SHARPEST VERSION OF THE 'DISTRICT LETTERS ARE LOCAL VOCABULARY' POINT. The same three characters denote an airport-industrial district in one jurisdiction, a retired mining district in another, and nothing at all in a third. Anyone normalising district codes across the valley — which is exactly what a national template does — produces confident nonsense. ⚠️ Kuna's M-3 is consolidated, not merely unused: say it no longer operates, not that it was 'deleted'. ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-09-10 from three meanings to FOUR. Eagle's M-3 is Extractive Industrial, which was missed when the claim was first written from three jurisdictions. The correction matters beyond the count: Eagle's M-3 and Kuna's former M-3 are both mining districts, so two of the four are near-siblings while Ada County's airport-industrial usage is unrelated to either. A reader could reasonably have inferred a pattern from three data points that the fourth breaks.

claims.claim: Star's 15-foot minimum setback next to a residential use or zone is not absolute. The same footnote allows a waiver to be requested where the adjacent property has the potential to redevelop as a non-residential use in the future.
claims.quotedLanguage: A waiver may be requested if thee adjacent property has the potential to redevelop as a non-residential use in the future.
claims.notes: ⚠️ CORRECTS A LIVE PAGE. The industrial page stated Star's 15-foot floor flatly, which is the same error class we correctly avoided on Star's 300-foot separation — reporting a constraint without its escape. A waiver may be REQUESTED; that is not the same as granted, and the page must not imply either that the floor is absolute or that a waiver is available on demand. ⚠️ QUOTE THE TYPO. The code reads 'if thee adjacent property'. It is the code's own error and the quote will not re-match the cache if it is silently corrected.

claims.claim: Meridian's own dimensional table says it can be overridden. Setback, landscape buffer, building height and parking standards within an adopted specific area plan take precedence over the standards in the table. Where an adjacent property is vacant, the Director determines its designation from the Comprehensive Plan, so even the input to a buffer requirement can be a matter of judgement rather than a fact on the ground.
claims.quotedLanguage: Dimensional standards for setbacks, landscape buffers, building heights, and parking requirements within adopted specific area plans take precedence over standards provided in this table.
claims.notes: A FOURTH KIND OF DISPLACEMENT — after proximity to housing (Boise, Star, Kuna), the building's own height (Eagle), and the use on the parcel (Eagle condition C), this is displacement by an OVERLYING PLAN. And again Meridian states it rather than us inferring it. ⚠️ Says nothing about which parcels sit inside an adopted specific area plan, or what any such plan requires — neither has been read. It establishes only that a plan can take precedence. ⚠️ The vacant-neighbour provision is worth stating carefully: the Director determining a designation from the Comprehensive Plan is a normal administrative mechanism, not a criticism, and must never be written as though it were arbitrary.

claims.claim: Meridian's six commercial districts do not share a height standard. Maximum building height runs 35 feet in C-N Neighborhood Business and L-O Limited Office, 50 feet in C-C Community Business, 65 feet in C-G General Retail and Service Commercial and in M-E Mixed Employment, and 95 feet in H-E High Density Employment — a range of nearly three to one across districts a seller would think of as simply commercial.
claims.quotedLanguage: Maximum building height (in feet) 35 50 65 35 65 95
claims.notes: ⚠️ The figures are read positionally from the table's column order C-N, C-C, C-G, L-O, M-E, H-E, which the same table states in its header row. Re-check the column order before amending this claim — a positional read is the fragile kind. ⚠️ The same table's setback row is NOT uniform in the same way: front, rear and interior side are 0 across the districts except L-O, which reads '10/5' under a note limiting the minimum to reuse of an existing residential structure. ⚠️ TOPICS TIGHTENED 2026-09-10. It was tagged 'land' as well, which was over-generous: a building-height table is not a claim about land. Over-tagging is not harmless — the eligibility gate treats a claim two candidates can both use as differentiating neither, so a loose topic silently destroys the claim's value to every page.

claims.claim: Meridian's commercial districts carry a street landscape buffer that scales with the classification of the road a property fronts, not with the district: 10 feet on a local street, 20 on a collector, 25 on an arterial, 35 on an entryway corridor and 50 along the interstate. A separate landscape buffer applies to adjacent residential uses, at 20 to 25 feet depending on the district.
claims.quotedLanguage: Street landscape buffer (in feet): Local 10 Collector 20 Arterial 25 Entryway corridor 35 Interstate 50
claims.notes: A FIFTH KIND OF CONSTRAINT and the least intuitive one yet: the usable area of a commercial parcel scales with the ROAD IT FRONTS. Two identical parcels in the same district give up 10 feet or 50 feet depending on whether they face a local street or the interstate — and the interstate frontage that makes a site visible is the one that costs the most land. ⚠️ A buffer is not a setback; do not conflate them or add them together. ⚠️ Setbacks here are measured from the ULTIMATE right-of-way for the street classification on the adopted transportation plan, not from today's property line, which is a separate trap on a road planned for widening. ⚠️ TOPIC 'land' REMOVED for the same reason as the height claim, though assetClass keeps land because a buffer genuinely consumes parcel area. The distinction matters: assetClass says who the claim is ABOUT, topic says what it is about, and only topic drives differentiation.

claims.claim: Commercial district letters do not correspond across Treasure Valley cities, in either direction. Eagle's C-2 is General Business, for commercial uses more intensive than those permitted in its other commercial zones; Garden City's C-2 is a mixed use commercial district; Star and Kuna both use C-2 for a commercial district of their own definition. The same idea also travels under different letters: a neighbourhood-scale business district is C-1 in Eagle and C-N in Meridian. Meridian's commercial set is C-N, C-C, C-G, L-O, M-E and H-E; Eagle's is L-O, C-1, C-2, C-3 and CBD.
claims.quotedLanguage: C-2 GENERAL BUSINESS DISTRICT: To permit the establishment of areas for commercial uses allowed in other commercial zones and commercial uses which are more intensive than those permitted in other commercial zones.
claims.notes: The commercial counterpart to the M-3 finding, and it fails in both directions at once: the same letters carry different meanings, AND the same meaning travels under different letters. That second half is the more dangerous one for a search-driven business, because a page written about 'C-2 commercial property' is writing about a different thing in each city while appearing to be about one. ⚠️ Says nothing about whether the districts permit similar USES — only that the labels do not correspond. Never infer a permitted use from a district letter across a city limit.

claims.claim: Eagle's L-O Limited Office district exists for groupings of professional, research, executive, administrative, accounting, clerical, stenographic, limited commercial and similar uses, and specifies that development shall not be traffic intensive.
claims.quotedLanguage: L-O LIMITED OFFICE DISTRICT: To permit the establishment of groupings of professional, research, executive, administrative, accounting, clerical, stenographic, limited commercial and similar uses.
claims.notes: One of very few claims we hold that is about OFFICE specifically rather than about commercial property generally — note the traffic-intensity condition, which is a use constraint rather than a dimensional one. Meridian also has an L-O and it caps height at 35 ft, the lowest in its commercial set alongside C-N. ⚠️ Do not assume the two cities' L-O districts permit the same uses; the letters matching is exactly the trap recorded in commercial-district-letters-do-not-correspond.
